progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: s01 (reading routine, annotation layer) and s02 (verb meanings; describe against explain). Biology: B10 (incomplete dominance in snapdragons, co-dominance in roan cattle, heterozygote phenotypes), B5a and B5b (sister chromatids, homologous pairs, one homologue from each parent). Chemistry: M6 C05 (strong and weak acids; extent of ionisation; strength against concentration), C12 (titration: moles from volume and concentration; 1 : 1 mole ratio for a monoprotic acid and NaOH), Year 11 acid and metal reactions, electrical conductivity of ionic solutions.
progression.startsWith: Comparisons written as two separate descriptions. The video opens: Here's a habit NESA's marking feedback keeps flagging. In eight of the last twelve Chemistry and Biology reports, it points out comparisons written as two separate descriptions: everything about one thing, then everything about the other. Each half can be right, and the answer still doesn't compare.
progression.stopsAfter: the three verb meanings; pairs on the same feature; the table-to-sentence trick; comparison words and the matched-feature check; a weak against strong compare; one Chemistry compare drill and one Biology distinguish drill.

teaching.task: When a question asks you to compare, contrast or distinguish, what makes the answer actually compare?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) NESA marking feedback flags comparisons written as two separate descriptions in eight of the last twelve Chemistry and Biology reports, and compare questions were worth three to six marks (1); (2) the three verbs with their paraphrased glossary meanings: compare takes similarities or differences, contrast and distinguish want differences (2); (3) one HSC-style Biology question compares snapdragon and roan cattle crosses (3); (4) the routine reads the verb, the marks and the givens: true-breeding parents differ, so every offspring is heterozygous (4); (5) a pair table puts one feature per row across both cases (5); (6) each row becomes one paired sentence with a comparison word: both heterozygotes look unlike either parent, so neither allele completely masks the other (6); (7) comparison words do the comparing, but cannot rescue a mismatched pair (7); (8) two correct descriptions still leave the comparing to the marker (8); (9) the guidelines rewarded complete pairing of the features asked about, not length (9); two drills with feedback (10 to 13); decision rule and handoff (14); key notes (15).
teaching.conversationalApproach: one fault carries the video: NESA keeps flagging comparisons written as two separate descriptions. One HSC-style Biology question (snapdragons and roan cattle) holds the content still while the answer is built: the routine reads the givens, a tiny pair table lines up one feature per row, and each row becomes one paired sentence with both or whereas, with a mark counter. A mismatched pair and a weak two-description answer show what fails, and the guidelines show what the marks followed. Two drills, one per subject, practise the shape.
teaching.openingDecision: Here's a habit NESA's marking feedback keeps flagging. In eight of the last twelve Chemistry and Biology reports, it points out comparisons written as two separate descriptions: everything about one thing, then everything about the other. Each half can be right, and the answer still doesn't compare. In recent Biology papers, compare questions were worth three to six marks. So let's learn to write in pairs.
teaching.understandingCheck: the narration says "Do the one in your subject, or both". Drill 1, Chemistry, compare, 3 marks: 0.10 mol L-1 hydrochloric acid against 0.10 mol L-1 ethanoic acid: conductivity, reaction with magnesium ribbon and the volume of 0.10 mol L-1 sodium hydroxide needed to neutralise 20.0 mL. Constraints "Using the data" and "in terms of acid strength". It has a surprising similarity (the same 20.0 mL) and two differences, so it trains both halves. Content: M6 C05 (strong and weak; extent of ionisation), C12 (titration and mole ratio), Year 11 reactions of acids with metals. Crossed habit: "Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid that reacts quickly. Ethanoic acid is a weak acid that reacts slowly." (two descriptions; no similarity). Drill 2, Biology, distinguish, 2 marks: homologous chromosomes against sister chromatids, with a painted chromosome-pair diagram. Content: B5a and B5b. It trains "differences only, still in pairs". Crossed habit: two stand-alone definitions with no feature they differ in.
teaching.curriculumScope: No syllabus dotpoint (skills video, HSC exam skills series): the NESA glossary of key words (paraphrased) and the Working Scientifically skill Communicating (NSW Chemistry and Biology Stage 6 syllabuses, 2017). starts at "comparisons written as two separate descriptions". It stops after the meanings of compare, contrast and distinguish, writing in pairs, the table-to-sentence trick, comparison words and the matched-feature check, a weak against strong compare, and two drills. It does not cover judgement verbs (s04), calculations (s05) or graph trends (s06).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. the shared skills kit (`src/explainer/lessons/skills-shared/`): `QuestionCard` with its annotation layer (`Ann` kinds verb, marks, given, constraint, ring, tag; `CardDim` for dimming parts), `MarksBadge`, `AnswerBox` (rows, margin ticks, counter, slots, `AAnn` under and ring), `MarkCounter`, `LostMarksTag`, `WeakStrongPanel`, `RoutineStrip` (mini at the far left; `none` tag on row 4 in the worked question), `DrillCountdown`, `Chip`, `GreyTag`, `CrossedHabit`, `PenArrow`, `Plate` and `mkPlate`, `Heading`, `HandLine`, `Flag`, `KeyNotes`, `Fade`, `DrawSquiggle`. New lesson-local components (suggested folder `src/explainer/lessons/skills-s03`): `PairTable`: a hand-drawn three-column table (feature, case A, case B) whose rows write on one at a time; a row can glow, dim or send a `PenArrow` down to an answer row. Built from `HandLine`, `DrawPath` and `Chip`. `PairLines`: thin amber links drawn between the matching clauses of two answer rows or two columns (used to show "paired" against "unpaired"). Built from `PenArrow` with `head={false}`. `HairZoom`: two magnified circles, one over the roan coat (separate coded hair strokes, each fully red or fully white) and one over a pink petal (an even pink wash). The logic is ported from B10's scene 8 zoom and redrawn in this kit's style. Plates: snapdragon red, white and pink; cattle red, white and roan (`COW` in `plates.ts`); B5 chromosome pair; M6 beaker (twice). New `mkPlate` entries are needed for the snapdragons, the chromosome pair and the beaker (alpha boxes measured 21 Oct; see Assets). No people, hands or faces.
design.transitionPlan: The report-tile grid opens and the two squiggle blocks slide into paired columns; the verb cards build with their count chips; the question card writes on with the cross plates in the side column; each annotation lands on its cue and adds a routine strip row; the pair table draws row by row with pair lines and brief hair and petal zoom circles; pen arrows carry each row into the answer box, which fills with ticks and the mark counter; the word trays build and the mismatched chip is crossed; the weak answer slides in beside the strong one; the guideline frame and bar clear one at a time; each drill clears the board and its feedback annotates the card before the model answer writes; the decision rule card and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
